content: The average age of participants in the reviewed trials ranged from 69 to 88 years, with 94% of the trials reporting a mean age of over 70 years. All trials were conducted in high-income countries. The duration of the trials varied between 5 and 36 months. Eight trials implemented individualized exercise interventions delivered at participants' homes. In most trials, the mean age of participants exceeded 80 years, with follow-up periods ranging from 5 to 24 months. There is limited moderate-quality evidence suggesting that t’ai chi training may reduce the risk of falls in older adults. However, the benefit of t’ai chi in reducing fall rates was observed only in individuals not preselected for a higher risk of falling. No significant effect was noted in those identified as being at higher risk of falls. Therefore, t’ai chi appears to be more effective in individuals who are not at high risk of falling. Adequate low-quality evidence indicates that multifactorial interventions can reduce fall rates in older adults at risk of falls. Nineteen trials examined the benefits of multifactorial interventions, which included assessments and referrals or active interventions. The mean age of participants in these trials was over 75 years, with follow-up periods ranging from 3 to 18 months. The proportion of female participants ranged from 49% to 100%. Only one study was conducted in a middle-income country (Thailand), while the remaining 18 trials were conducted in high-income countries, including Australia, Canada, China, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Limited moderate-quality evidence suggests that home safety assessments and tailored interventions can reduce fall rates in older adults at risk of falls. Six randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 4,208 participants investigated the effectiveness of home safety interventions. The mean age of participants was over 75 years, with follow-up periods ranging from 3 to 18 months. Post-hoc analysis revealed that home safety interventions delivered by occupational therapists were more effective than those delivered by other healthcare professionals. There is very limited low-quality evidence suggesting that medication reviews and the modification or withdrawal of harmful medications may reduce the risk of falls in older adults. However, an educational program for general practitioners focusing on medication review and treatment modification was found to be ineffective in reducing fall rates. Falls are a significant clinical outcome, valued as important by older adults, their families, and caregivers. The guideline development group strongly believes that fall prevention recommendations will be valued by healthcare providers and accepted by stakeholders, including older adults and their caregivers. Fall-prevention interventions are resource-intensive. However, the health benefits gained from these interventions are likely to outweigh the resource burden. Costs can be reduced through task shifting, involving family members, and delivering interventions in group settings. While multifactorial interventions may be challenging to implement due to the involvement of multiple service providers, home-based individual interventions may serve as an alternative. Some trials have successfully utilized non-specialized healthcare professionals to deliver fall-prevention interventions, suggesting feasibility in both highand low-resource healthcare settings. The guideline development group strongly believes that all fall-prevention recommendations will improve health equity. However, most trials were conducted in high-income countries, and further research is needed to assess the feasibility of implementing fall-prevention interventions in lowand middle-income countries. There is also a pressing need to standardize fall-risk assessments to identify high-risk older adults. Currently, fall history is the most commonly used factor in trials, with only a small proportion of studies incorporating additional risk factors. Vision care for older adults at risk of falls should not be limited to cataract surgery. Due to the high variability in multifactorial interventions, they were rated as low quality. This variability stems from differences in the components of interventions and the targeted risk factors for reducing falls. Future research should aim to disentangle multifactorial interventions and report treatment effects by subgroups of intervention components. The guideline development group recommends the following interventions for older adults at risk of falls: 1. Medication review and withdrawal of unnecessary or harmful medications (low-quality evidence, conditional recommendation). 2. Multimodal exercise programs focusing on balance, strength, flexibility, and functional training (moderate-quality evidence, strong recommendation). 3. Home modifications to remove environmental hazards following a specialist’s assessment (moderate-quality evidence, strong recommendation). 4. Multifactorial interventions integrating assessments with individually tailored interventions (low-quality evidence, conditional recommendation). Effective primary healthcare interventions for fall prevention use various approaches to identify individuals at increased risk. However, no evidence-based tool exists to accurately identify older adults at high risk of falling. Most trials rely on fall history, with only a few incorporating additional risk factors. Future research should focus on standardizing risk assessments and exploring the feasibility of implementing fall-prevention strategies in low-resource settings.
